facts.statement: Acamptonectes fossils date to the Hauterivian stage of the Early Cretaceous.
facts.quote: fossil_range: Hauterivian~

facts.statement: The first specimen of Acamptonectes was found in Speeton, England, in 1958, but the genus was not formally described until 2012.
facts.quote: The first specimen, a partial adult skeleton, was discovered in Speeton, England, in 1958, but was not formally described until 2012 by Valentin Fischer and colleagues.

facts.statement: A partial subadult skeleton of Acamptonectes was identified from Cremlingen, Germany, along with specimens from other English localities.
facts.quote: They also recognised a partial subadult skeleton belonging to the genus from Cremlingen, Germany, and specimens from other localities in England.

facts.statement: Acamptonectes is estimated to have reached a length of 3 meters.
facts.quote: A small ichthyosaur, Acamptonectes is estimated to have been 3 m long.

facts.statement: The genus name refers to adaptations that made the animal's trunk rigid, including tightly fitting skull bones and interlocking vertebrae.
facts.quote: The generic name refers to unusual adaptations in the body of Acamptonectes that made its trunk rigid, including tightly fitting bones in the occiput (back and lower part of the skull) and interlocking vertebral centra

facts.statement: Acamptonectes possessed large eye sockets and a tail fluke typical of ichthyosaurs.
facts.quote: As an ichthyosaur, Acamptonectes had large eye sockets and a tail fluke.

facts.statement: Researchers suggest Acamptonectes was likely a generalist predator, despite having eyes adapted for depth diving.
facts.quote: Although the larger eyes of Acamptonectes would have made it better adapted than platypterygiines to depth diving, it was probably a generalist predator.

facts.statement: Acamptonectes fed on soft, fleshy prey like fish and squid using slender, ridged teeth adapted for impaling.
facts.quote: Its teeth, which were slender and textured with longitudinal ridges, were adapted for impaling prey, which suggests it likely fed on soft, fleshy prey such as fish and squid.

facts.statement: The initial specimen was collected in 1958 by students and a technician from Hull University in the Speeton Clay Formation.
facts.quote: Over a series of weekends in 1958, four students and a technician from Hull University's geology department collected a fossil specimen from the Speeton Clay Formation at Speeton in northern England.

facts.statement: The original specimen was transferred to the Hunterian Museum at the University of Glasgow in 1991.
facts.quote: In 1991, it was transferred to the Hunterian Museum of the University of Glasgow (GLAHM) when the geology department of Hull University was closed.

facts.statement: Robert M. Appleby described the specimen as Platypterygius speetoni in an unpublished monograph before his death in 2003.
facts.quote: Palaeontologist Robert M. Appleby described the specimen and assigned it to the genus Platypterygius as the species "P. speetoni" (which he considered primitive within that genus), in a monograph that remained unpublished at the time of his death in 2003.

facts.statement: A second specimen was discovered in 1985 in the Speeton Clay and is now catalogued at the Natural History Museum, London.
facts.quote: A second specimen of the species was found in 1985, also in the Speeton Clay, and is catalogued as NHMUK R11185 at the Natural History Museum, London (NHMUK).

facts.statement: A German specimen was discovered in 2005 by private collector Hans-Dieter Macht during construction work.
facts.quote: This German specimen was discovered in 2005 when private fossil collector Hans-Dieter Macht found some vertebrae in a construction area.

facts.statement: The German specimen was prepared and mounted in 2005 at the State Natural History Museum of Braunschweig.
facts.quote: It was prepared and mounted in 2005 at the museum, where it is catalogued as SNHM1284-R.

facts.statement: The genus and species Acamptonectes densus were formally named in 2012 by a team led by Valentin Fischer.
facts.quote: In 2012, a team of palaeontologists led by Fischer formally named the new genus and species Acamptonectes densus.

facts.statement: The name Acamptonectes densus translates to "rigid swimmer" and "compact" or "tightly packed".
facts.quote: The generic name is derived from the Greek words akamptos and nektes, which together mean "rigid swimmer"; the specific name means "compact" or "tightly packed".

facts.statement: In 2012, several bones from the Cambridge Greensand Formation were tentatively assigned to an uncertain species of Acamptonectes.
facts.quote: Multiple basioccipitals (a bone at the lower part of the occiput), stapes (one of the ear bones), and a basisphenoid (a bone within the lower part of the braincase) from the Cambridge Greensand Formation of Cambridge, England, were also assigned to Acamptonectes sp. (i.e., an uncertain species within the genus Acamptonectes) by Fischer and colleagues in 2012.

facts.statement: In 2014, researchers identified bones from Ophthalmosaurus in rocks dating between 145 and 139.8 million years old, leading to a re-evaluation of earlier specimens.
facts.quote: In 2014, Fischer and colleagues identified a basioccipital and humerus belonging to Ophthalmosaurus (or a closely related ichthyosaur) from Berriasian-aged rocks (dating to between 145 and 139.8 million years old) near Nettleton, Lincolnshire.

facts.statement: Ferdinand Broili named a specimen Ichthyosaurus brunsvicensis in 1909 but considered the assignment tentative.
facts.quote: In 1909, German palaeontologist Ferdinand Broili named it as a new species of the genus Ichthyosaurus, Ichthyosaurus brunsvicensis, but considered its assignment to the genus tentative.

facts.statement: Broili's specimen consisted of a skull base and interclavicle but was destroyed during World War II.
facts.quote: Broili's specimen consisted of an incomplete basicranium (skull base) and an incomplete interclavicle (a bone between the clavicles, or collar bones); however, the specimen was destroyed during World War II.

facts.statement: Researchers suggested the Hannover specimen was a juvenile Acamptonectes or a related animal based on its basicranium.
facts.quote: They found it similar in several features to Acamptonectes but also different in others; they suggested the specimen was a juvenile because of the size and shape of its basicranium.

facts.statement: The name Ichthyosaurus brunsvicensis is considered a nomen dubium due to the fragmentary nature of the specimen.
facts.quote: Due to its fragmentary and inaccessible nature, they considered I. brunsvicensis a nomen dubium (dubious name).

facts.statement: Acamptonectes challenged the belief that only platypterygiines survived the Jurassic–Cretaceous boundary extinction.
facts.quote: The discovery of Acamptonectes had significant implications for the evolutionary history of ichthyosaurs. The generalised platypterygiine ophthalmosaurids were long believed to be the only lineage of ichthyosaurs that survived into the Early Cretaceous following a mass extinction of ichthyosaurs across the Jurassic–Cretaceous boundary.

facts.statement: The discovery of Acamptonectes provides evidence against a mass extinction of ichthyosaurs at the Jurassic–Cretaceous boundary.
facts.quote: As one of the first-known ophthalmosaurine ophthalmosaurids from the Early Cretaceous, the discovery of Acamptonectes provided evidence against such a mass extinction.

facts.statement: Acamptonectes was morphologically similar to the earlier ophthalmosaurines Ophthalmosaurus and Mollesaurus.
facts.quote: Acamptonectes was similar in morphology to the related but earlier fellow ophthalmosaurines Ophthalmosaurus and Mollesaurus.

facts.statement: While the color of Acamptonectes is unknown, some ichthyosaurs may have been uniformly dark in life, supported by evidence of eumelanin pigments in early ichthyosaur skin fossils.
facts.quote: Although the colour of Acamptonectes is unknown, at least some ichthyosaurs may have been uniformly dark-coloured in life, which is evidenced by the discovery of high concentrations of eumelanin pigments in the preserved skin of an early ichthyosaur fossil.

facts.statement: The holotype of Acamptonectes is considered an adult due to extensive bone fusion, including within the occiput, and a smooth humerus texture, making it larger than other members of the family Ophthalmosauridae.
facts.quote: The holotype and specimen NHMUK R11185 are large compared to other members of the wider family Ophthalmosauridae; the holotype is thought to have been an adult because of the extensive fusion of its bones, including within the occiput, and the smooth texture of the humerus.

facts.statement: The Acamptonectes snout had a depth-to-length ratio of 0.044, which is one of the lowest among ophthalmosaurids.
facts.quote: The snout was also only 0.044 times as deep as it was long, one of the lowest ratios among ophthalmosaurids.

facts.statement: The quadrate bone in Acamptonectes was C-shaped when viewed from the side, forming the jaw joint.
facts.quote: When viewed from the side, the quadrate bone, which connected to the lower jaw to form the jaw joint, was C-shaped.

facts.statement: The stapes in Acamptonectes had a uniquely slender shaft and a large, square head, features that distinguish the genus from related ichthyosaurs.
facts.quote: The stapes had a shaft that was more slender than in any other ichthyosaur, and its head was large and square; these features are regarded as an autapomorphy—a characteristic that distinguishes the genus from related genera.

facts.statement: The basisphenoid in Acamptonectes possessed a well-developed crest on its upper surface, an autapomorphy distinct from the wide, flat plateau found in other ichthyosaur species.
facts.quote: The basisphenoid had a well-developed crest on its upper surface; this is considered another autapomorphy because this surface was a wide, flat plateau in other ichthyosaur species.

facts.statement: In Acamptonectes, the basisphenoid was fused to the parasphenoid at its front end with no visible suture between the two bones.
facts.quote: At its front end, the basisphenoid was fused to the parasphenoid (another bone within the lower part of the braincase) and no suture (border between the two bones) can be seen.

facts.statement: The midline canal of the basioccipital in Acamptonectes had a bilobed appearance when viewed from above due to bordering ridges, an autapomorphy of the genus.
facts.quote: The midline canal that formed this floor was bordered by ridges, giving a bilobed appearance when seen from above; this is also regarded as an autapomorphy of the genus.

facts.statement: The occipital condyle in Acamptonectes was separated from the rest of the bone by a constricted band, a feature unlike most other ophthalmosaurids.
facts.quote: The occipital condyle was well-demarcated from the remainder of the bone by a constricted band, unlike most other ophthalmosaurids.

facts.statement: The paroccipital processes in Acamptonectes were elongated and slender, contrasting with the short and stout processes found in other ophthalmosaurids.
facts.quote: The opisthotics, which are on either side of the basioccipital, possessed extensions called the paroccipital processes which pointed backwards and upwards. These processes were elongated and slender in Acamptonectes and Ophthalmosaurus, but short and stout in other ophthalmosaurids.

facts.statement: Acamptonectes teeth had striated bases and quadrangular roots, but were not square like those of Platypterygius.
facts.quote: The teeth of Acamptonectes had striated bases and quadrangular roots, as in numerous ophthalmosaurids, but they were not square like those of Platypterygius.

facts.statement: Resorption pits found on the roots of specimen SNHM1284-R indicate that the teeth of Acamptonectes were still growing.
facts.quote: Some of the roots of SNHM1284-R had resorption pits, indicating its teeth were still growing.

facts.statement: The known complete tooth crown of Acamptonectes was small, slender, and sharply pointed, resembling teeth from the rear of the jaw in Baptanodon.
facts.quote: The only-known complete tooth crown was small compared to those of other ophthalmosaurids; it was also slender and sharply pointed, and similar to the teeth from the rear of the jaw in Baptanodon.

facts.statement: The bottom two-thirds of the Acamptonectes tooth crown featured subtle longitudinal ridges and a coarse texture finer than that found in Aegirosaurus and some Platypterygius specimens.
facts.quote: The bottom two-thirds of the crown had subtle, longitudinal ridges and was covered in a coarse texture that was nevertheless finer than those in Aegirosaurus and some Platypterygius specimens.

facts.statement: Acamptonectes possessed disc-shaped vertebrae that were deeply concave on both ends, a trait typical of ichthyosaurs.
facts.quote: As was typical for ichthyosaurs, the vertebral centra of Acamptonectes were disc-shaped and deeply concave on both ends.

facts.statement: The bony projections on Acamptonectes vertebrae were greatly reduced to adapt to its fully aquatic lifestyle.
facts.quote: The processes (bony projections that serve as muscle and rib attachments) projecting from the centra were greatly reduced as an adaptation for its fully aquatic lifestyle.

facts.statement: Acamptonectes had short, high front neck vertebrae that became progressively longer in the trunk region.
facts.quote: In Acamptonectes, the front-most cervical (neck) centra were high and short, and the following cervical and dorsal (trunk) centra become progressively longer.

facts.statement: The first tail vertebra of Acamptonectes was 3.12 times as high as it was long.
facts.quote: the first caudal (tail) vertebra, which was 3.12 times as high as it was long.

facts.statement: The first two neck vertebrae (atlas and axis) of Acamptonectes were fused into a single wide complex.
facts.quote: The first two cervicals—the atlas and axis—were fused into a single complex that was wide when viewed from the rear.

facts.statement: Acamptonectes had unique dorsal vertebrae that were tightly interlocking and featured extensive ridges on their rear surfaces.
facts.quote: The centra of the dorsal vertebrae were autapomorphic, being tightly interlocking and having extensive posterolateral lamellae (ridges lining the rear surfaces of the centra).

facts.statement: Pitted surfaces on the neural spines of Acamptonectes suggest they were covered in cartilage.
facts.quote: The top surfaces of the neural spines were often pitted, indicating they had a cartilage covering.

facts.statement: Acamptonectes had robust ribs with a round cross-section, unlike the "8"-shaped ribs found in other thunnosaurian ichthyosaurs.
facts.quote: The ribs were distinct in being robust with a round cross-section; this contrasted with the "8"-shaped cross-section that is seen in other thunnosaurian ichthyosaurs.

facts.statement: Acamptonectes had a shoulder blade similar to Ophthalmosaurus that was strongly compressed side-to-side, unlike the thick, rod-like shaft of P. hercynicus.
facts.quote: The scapula (shoulder blade) of Acamptonectes was similar to that of Ophthalmosaurus. It was strongly compressed from side to side, unlike that in P. hercynicus, in which the shaft was thick and rod-like.

facts.statement: The finger bones in Acamptonectes flippers were oval and tapered away from the body with irregular, slightly concave edges.
facts.quote: The phalanx bones (finger bones within the flipper) were oval as in Ophthalmosaurus, Arthropterygius, and some species of Brachypterygius; they tapered away from the body, and the edges of the peripheral phalanx bones were irregular and slightly concave.

facts.statement: Researchers suggest the long neural spines of Acamptonectes may be bony extensions analogous to extraneural processes found in juvenile Stenopterygius.
facts.quote: These long spines may be bony extensions that are analogous to the extraneural processes, a row of bones located above the tops of the neural spines that are preserved in two juvenile Stenopterygius specimens.

facts.statement: A 2012 study classified Acamptonectes as a member of the family Ophthalmosauridae.
facts.quote: In 2012, a phylogenetic analysis conducted by Fischer and colleagues found Acamptonectes to be a member of the family Ophthalmosauridae

facts.statement: A 2012 phylogenetic analysis found Acamptonectes most closely related to Ophthalmosaurus natans.
facts.quote: In 2012, Fischer and colleagues found that it grouped closest with "Ophthalmosaurus" natans

facts.statement: A 2019 analysis suggested Acamptonectes was more closely related to Janusaurus, Keilhauia, and Palvennia than to other ophthalmosaurines.
facts.quote: In 2019, another analysis by the same authors found Acamptonectes closer to Janusaurus, Keilhauia, and Palvennia than to Paraophthalmosaurus

facts.statement: Phylogenetic analyses of Acamptonectes have often yielded low statistical support for its specific placement within the family.
facts.quote: In each case, however, the Bremer support—a measure of the likelihood of a phylogenetic tree's arrangement over alternatives—of the groupings was low.

facts.statement: A 2016 study placed Acamptonectes in an unresolved group (polytomy) alongside several other ophthalmosaurines.
facts.quote: In 2016, Fischer and colleagues found Ophthalmosaurinae to consist of Mollesaurus as the sister group to a polytomy including O. icenicus, "O." natans, Leninia, Acamptonectes, and a group containing Cryopterygius, Janusaurus, and Palvennia.

facts.statement: A 2020 analysis placed Acamptonectes in an unresolved relationship with Ophthalmosaurus icenicus, Leninia, and Athabascasaurus.
facts.quote: In their 2020 description of Arthropterygius thalassonotus, Lisandro Campos and colleagues placed Acamptonectes in a polytomy with O. icenicus, Leninia, and Athabascasaurus

facts.statement: Acamptonectes is significant because it proves ophthalmosaurine ichthyosaurs survived the Jurassic-Cretaceous boundary extinction event.
facts.quote: Acamptonectes is a significant find because it is an ophthalmosaurine from the Early Cretaceous, demonstrating the ophthalmosaurines were not entirely wiped out at the Jurassic–Cretaceous boundary.

facts.statement: Acamptonectes lived during the Early Cretaceous period.
facts.quote: Acamptonectes is a significant find because it is an ophthalmosaurine from the Early Cretaceous

facts.statement: Studies indicate a net extinction rate of zero for ophthalmosaurids at the Jurassic-Cretaceous boundary.
facts.quote: The Jurassic–Cretaceous boundary had a net extinction rate of 0 and even the highest survival rates.

facts.statement: Acamptonectes possessed a dolphin-like body shape that made it better adapted to aquatic life than other marine reptiles.
facts.quote: With their dolphin-like bodies, ichthyosaurs were better adapted to their aquatic environment than any other group of marine reptiles.

facts.statement: Acamptonectes swam using a thunniform method, which is faster and more efficient than the eel-like swimming of earlier ichthyosaurs.
facts.quote: Jurassic and Cretaceous ichthyosaurs, including Acamptonectes, had evolved a thunniform method of swimming rather than the anguilliform (undulating or eel-like) methods of earlier species.

facts.statement: The thunniform swimming style of Acamptonectes allowed it to live an open-ocean lifestyle and swim faster than similarly sized marine reptiles.
facts.quote: Thunniform ichthyosaurs were able to swim faster and more efficiently than other marine reptiles of similar sizes, and were better adapted to a pelagic (open-ocean) lifestyle.

facts.statement: Acamptonectes had compact bodies and crescent-shaped tail fins that aided its swimming.
facts.quote: Their swimming was aided by their compact bodies and crescent-shaped tail fins.

facts.statement: Most of Acamptonectes' skeleton was unusually rigid, severely limiting side-to-side motion in the front part of its body.
facts.quote: Most of the skeleton of Acamptonectes appears to have been unusually rigid, which would have severely limited the extent of side-to-side motion in the front part of the skeleton.

facts.statement: The holotype of Acamptonectes was found in the D2D beds, while another specimen came from the slightly older D2C beds.
facts.quote: The Acamptonectes holotype came from the D2D beds and the specimen NHMUK R11185 came from the slightly older D2C beds.

facts.statement: The articulated nature of the Acamptonectes holotype indicates it genuinely originated from the Hauterivian rather than being reworked from older rocks.
facts.quote: The holotype of Acamptonectes is partially articulated, as were some nearby crinoid fossils, indicating the specimen was not reworked and genuinely came from the Hauterivian.

facts.statement: Oxygen isotope data suggests water temperatures in the Acamptonectes habitat ranged from 11°C to 15°C during the Hauterivian stage.
facts.quote: δ18O levels in belemnite fossils indicate the temperature of the Speeton Clay was about 11 C at the beginning of the Hauterivian, rose to 15 C during the middle part of this stage, and reverted to 11 C by its end.

facts.statement: A German specimen of Acamptonectes was found in late Hauterivian rocks near Cremlingen in the Lower Saxony Basin.
facts.quote: SNHM1284-R, the German specimen of Acamptonectes, comes from late Hauterivian rocks of the Lower Saxony Basin near Cremlingen in eastern Lower Saxony.

facts.statement: The rocks containing Acamptonectes in Germany were deposited in shallow seas during periods of rising and falling sea levels.
facts.quote: The late Hauterivian rocks of the region were deposited in the neritic zone (shallow seas) during a time of alternating marine transgression and regression (rising and falling sea levels).
